subject: sig_sotos_true.csv
text: The analysis found a perfect match to the Sotos syndrome signature, with an AUC of 1.0 and a Z-score of 125.4. All 500 submitted probes overlapped with the known Sotos syndrome signature, giving a Jaccard similarity of 0.07 and representing 100 % of the submitted probes. This result is limited to the study itself and does not imply it will transfer to other studies. The evidence and cohort ceilings are both described as strong, and no data were missing or refused. The next-closest match was Claes-Jensen syndrome, with a Z-score of 31.4.

subject: sig_sotos_flipped.csv
text: The analysis identified a perfect match to Sotos syndrome, with an AUC of 1.0 and a Z-score of 125.4. This result is limited to the study itself and does not imply it will transfer to other studies. The evidence and cohort size are both described as “Strong”. No result was refused.

subject: sig_tiny.csv

text: The analysis found a perfect match to Sotos syndrome, with an AUC of 1.0 and a Z-score of 26.3. All twenty submitted probes overlapped the known Sotos syndrome signature, representing 100 % of the submitted probes, though the Jaccard similarity is zero, indicating a possible re-derivation or subset of an existing signature. subject: sig_low_coverage.csv

text: The analysis was refused because none of the 500 submitted probes were present in any corpus cohort, so nothing could be scored. All 500 probes were missing, giving a 100 % missing rate. Only a tiny fraction of probes were found on the EPIC v1 platform (0.4 %) and the EPIC v2 platform contained all 500 probes but still did not meet the required coverage. The refusal code is “insufficient_probe_coverage”. No matches or scores were generated.

subject: Silver-Russell syndrome
text: The analysis looked at 63 cases of Silver-Russell syndrome using data from two studies, GSE104451 and GSE55491, and built a signature from 64 probes. The signature was successfully constructed from rederived, unpublished sources and was tested with a leave-one-study-out approach, where one direction was computed and the other was not. In the computed direction the test achieved a sensitivity of five out of eighteen and a specificity of six out of six. Overall the result was graded, and there was no evidence of a band at the typical case score. The control data came from within the same series, and the interpretation was made between studies.

subject: Sotos syndrome
text: The analysis found a strong result for Sotos syndrome, but the confounding gate failed. The study used 38 cases and 53 training controls from within the same series, based on a published probe list of 7,085 signatures. Only one study (GSE74432) contributed data, and the interpretation is limited to within-study only. The verdict is that the finding comes from a single-study analysis.

subject: Kabuki syndrome type 1
text: The analysis looked at Kabuki syndrome type 1 and found no evidence of a typical-case band-at-score. The study compared data from two separate experiments and used a rederived, unpublished signature based on 278 probes. A total of 37 cases and 20 training controls were included, and the signature was successfully built. The overall verdict was graded, with the interpretation scoped between the two studies.

subject: Down syndrome
text: The analysis was performed on a single study of Down syndrome, using 29 cases and an equal number of training controls from within the same series. A gene-expression signature was built from 3,753 probes, derived anew rather than taken from a published source. The overall score for a typical case was moderate, but the confounding gate failed, meaning the result is limited to the study itself. No leave-one-out directions were computed. The verdict is that the findings apply only within this single study.

subject: Williams syndrome
text: The analysis was performed on a single study (GSE66552) involving 20 cases of Williams syndrome and 15 training controls, using a rederived, unpublished signature based on 9,537 probes. The result was classified as “moderate” for the typical case score, but the confounding gate failed. The interpretation is limited to within-study only and the overall verdict is a single-study finding. No additional directions or further analyses were computed.

subject: CHARGE syndrome
text: The analysis supports an association with CHARGE syndrome. The result is limited to the single study GSE97362 and is intended for use only within that study. The test used 19 cases and 29 training controls, with a signature built from 907 probes. The confounding gate failed, and the interpretation is scoped to within-study only. No additional directions or further studies were involved.

At a typical case score the evidence band is Supporting, within one study only.

subject: ICF syndrome
text: The analysis gave a moderate score for the typical case. The study involved fifteen cases and ten training controls from within the same series, using data from a single study (GSE95040). The disorder examined was ICF syndrome, and the result is intended only for use within this study. The signature was successfully built from a rederived, unpublished source and included 7,740 probes. The confounding gate failed, meaning the result is not considered reliable beyond this study.

subject: 7q11.23 duplication syndrome
text: The analysis was performed on a moderate-scoring case of 7q11.23 duplication syndrome using data from a single study (GSE66552). The result is limited to the scope of that study and cannot be applied more broadly. The test used 10 cases and 15 control samples, with a signature built from 1,827 probes. The overall verdict is that the finding comes from a single-study analysis.

subject: Weaver syndrome
text: The analysis was aimed at Weaver syndrome but there were not enough cases to draw a conclusion. Only eight cases were available, with 53 control samples, and the study used data from GSE74432. Because the number of cases was insufficient, the result is reported as “too-few-cases”. No further interpretation or signature could be generated. The testing approach was considered not testable.

subject: Claes-Jensen syndrome
text: The analysis looked at Claes-Jensen syndrome using data from study GSE108423, with six cases and twelve training controls drawn from within the same series. The test was deemed not-testable because of confounding factors. The result was classified as “too-few-cases,” meaning there were insufficient cases to reach a conclusion. No signature was built and no additional directions were computed.
